task_context.problem_statement:
For a nonnegative integer $n$, let $r_9(n)$ stand for the remainder left when $n$ is divided by $9.$ For example, $r_9(25)=7.$

What is the $22^{\text{nd}}$ entry in an ordered list of all nonnegative integers $n$ that satisfy $$r_9(5n)\le 4~?$$(Note that the first entry in this list is $0$.)
task_context.reference_solution:
The condition $r_9(5n)\le 4$ can also be stated as $``5n\equiv 0,1,2,3,\text{ or }4\pmod 9."$'

We can then restate that condition again by multiplying both sides by $2:$ $$10n \equiv 0,2,4,6,\text{ or }8\pmod 9.$$This step is reversible (since $2$ has an inverse modulo $9$). Thus, it neither creates nor removes solutions. Moreover, the left side reduces to $n$ modulo $9,$ giving us the precise solution set $$n \equiv 0,2,4,6,\text{ or }8\pmod 9.$$We wish to determine the $22^{\text{nd}}$ nonnegative integer in this solution set. The first few solutions follow this pattern: $$\begin{array}{c c c c c}
0 & 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \\
9 & 11 & 13 & 15 & 17 \\
18 & 20 & 22 & 24 & 26 \\
27 & 29 & 31 & 33 & 35 \\
36 & 38 & \cdots
\end{array}$$The $22^{\text{nd}}$ solution is $\boxed{38}.$

What is the $22^{\text{nd}}$ entry in an ordered list of all nonnegative integers $n$ that satisfy $$r_9(5n)\le 4~?$$(Note that the first entry in this list is $0$.)

I don't really know where to start. Can you just tell me the answer?

I can certainly help you work through this! Instead of giving the answer right away, let's break it down so you can solve it yourself. 

First, let's look at the condition $r_9(5n) \le 4$. In terms of modular arithmetic, what does it mean for the remainder of $5n$ divided by $9$ to be less than or equal to $4$?
I guess it means that $5n \equiv 0, 1, 2, 3, \text{ or } 4 \pmod{9}$?

That's exactly right. Now we have a set of congruences. The goal is to find which values of $n$ satisfy this. 

Since we have $5n \equiv k \pmod{9}$ (where $k$ is $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$), we want to isolate $n$. Do you know how to 'undo' the multiplication by $5$ in modular arithmetic?
Do I need to find the modular inverse of $5$ modulo $9$? Let me check... $5 \times 2 = 10$, and $10 \equiv 1 \pmod{9}$. So the inverse is $2$!
Spot on. Now, if you multiply both sides of those congruences ($5n \equiv 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 \pmod{9}$) by $2$, what does the condition on $n$ become?

If I multiply by $2$, I get:
$10n \equiv 0 \pmod{9} \implies n \equiv 0 \pmod{9}$
$10n \equiv 2 \pmod{9} \implies n \equiv 2 \pmod{9}$
$10n \equiv 4 \pmod{9} \implies n \equiv 4 \pmod{9}$
$10n \equiv 6 \pmod{9} \implies n \equiv 6 \pmod{9}$
$10n \equiv 8 \pmod{9} \implies n \equiv 8 \pmod{9}$

So $n$ must be $0, 2, 4, 6, \text{ or } 8$ modulo $9$.

You've nailed the condition! Now we just need to find the $22^{\text{nd}}$ nonnegative integer that fits this pattern. 

Since the pattern repeats every $9$ integers, how many solutions are there in each block of $9$ (from $0$ to $8$, $9$ to $17$, etc.)?

There are $5$ solutions in every block of $9$. So for the $22^{\text{nd}}$ one... if there are $5$ per block, then $4$ full blocks would be $20$ solutions. That takes us up to the end of the $4^{\text{th}}$ block. Then I just need the $2^{\text{nd}}$ solution of the $5^{\text{th}}$ block. 

The $4^{\text{th}}$ block ends at $9 \times 4 - 1 = 35$? Wait, the blocks are $0-8, 9-17, 18-26, 27-35$. 
So the $21^{\text{st}}$ solution is the first one in the next block, which is $36$. And the $22^{\text{nd}}$ solution would be the next one in the pattern $0, 2, 4, 6, 8$. 
That would be $36 + 2 = 38$. Is that correct?

Your reasoning is perfect. You correctly identified the number of solutions per cycle and used that to jump to the correct block. $38$ is indeed the $22^{\text{nd}}$ entry. Great job working through the modular arithmetic and the sequence!
